questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AQA AS 3.1.2 Formula Mass and Numerical Reasoning
questions.question: Formula mass and ionic particle counting
questions.subtopic: Ionic formula mass, significant figures, limitation, hydrated salt and back titration
questions.prompt: A sample of calcium nitrate has formula Ca(NO₃)₂. Use Ar: Ca=40.1, N=14.0, O=16.0 and Nₐ=6.02×10²³ mol⁻¹. (a) Calculate its relative formula mass. (b) Calculate the mass of 0.0200 mol Ca(NO₃)₂. (c) Calculate the number of nitrate ions released if that amount completely dissociates in water. Explain why 'relative formula mass' is the correct term. [6 marks]
markPoints: Uses the term relative formula mass for an ionic substance rather than relative molecular mass.
States relative formula mass has no unit; the molar mass is 164.1 g mol⁻¹.
Computes sample mass 0.0200×164.1=3.282 g, quoted 3.28 g to 3 significant figures.
Uses two nitrate ions per Ca(NO₃)₂ formula unit, giving 0.0400 mol NO₃⁻.
Computes number of nitrate ions 0.0400×6.02×10²³=2.408×10²², quoted 2.41×10²².
questions.modelAnswer: Ionic Ca(NO₃)₂ consists of a repeating lattice, so the relative formula mass is 40.1+2(14.0+3×16.0)=164.1 (dimensionless). Its molar mass is 164.1 g mol⁻¹. The mass of 0.0200 mol is 3.282 g≈3.28 g. Each formula unit contains two nitrate ions, so n(NO₃⁻)=0.0400 mol; the number is 0.0400×6.02×10²³=2.408×10²²≈2.41×10²² nitrate ions.

questions.question: Precision-limited concentration and significant figures
questions.subtopic: Ionic formula mass, significant figures, limitation, hydrated salt and back titration
questions.prompt: A solute with molar mass 106.0 g mol⁻¹ has mass 0.683 g and is dissolved to a total volume of 25.0 cm³. (a) Calculate the amount in moles. (b) Find the concentration in mol dm⁻³. (c) Give your final answers with justified significant figures based on the measurements. [5 marks]
markPoints: Finds n=0.006443396… mol, reporting 0.00644 mol to 3 significant figures.
Converts 25.0 cm³ to 0.0250 dm³.
Uses c=n/V to get 0.257735… mol dm⁻³ and quotes 0.258 mol dm⁻³.
Explains the supplied mass and volume each have 3 significant figures and limit the precision of a product/quotient.
questions.modelAnswer: n=m/Mᵣ=0.683/106.0=0.006443396… mol≈0.00644 mol. V=25.0/1000=0.0250 dm³. c=n/V=(0.683/106.0)/0.0250=0.257735… mol dm⁻³≈0.258 mol dm⁻³. Both mass 0.683 g and volume 25.0 cm³ have 3 significant figures, so state the results to 3 significant figures, not the longer calculator display.

questions.question: Determine the limiting reagent and theoretical product mass
questions.subtopic: Ionic formula mass, significant figures, limitation, hydrated salt and back titration
questions.prompt: Magnesium reacts with oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. A mixture initially contains 0.300 mol Mg and 0.180 mol O₂. Use Ar Mg=24.3, O=16.0. Determine (a) the limiting reactant, (b) maximum amount and mass of MgO, and (c) moles of excess reactant remaining. Show the mole-ratio reasoning. [6 marks]
markPoints: Recognises the balanced reaction has Mg:O₂:MgO mole ratio 2:1:2.
Calculates oxygen required by 0.300 mol Mg is 0.150 mol O₂.
Identifies Mg as limiting reactant because 0.180 mol O₂ is present.
Finds theoretical MgO amount is 0.300 mol.
Calculates Mᵣ(MgO)=40.3 and theoretical mass 0.300×40.3=12.09 g≈12.1 g.
Finds leftover O₂ amount 0.180−0.150=0.0300 mol.
questions.modelAnswer: The balanced 2:1 ratio means 0.300 mol Mg requires 0.150 mol O₂. Since 0.180 mol O₂ is available, Mg is limiting. The 2Mg→2MgO ratio gives 0.300 mol MgO. Mᵣ(MgO)=24.3+16.0=40.3 and theoretical mass=0.300×40.3=12.09 g≈12.1 g. The excess oxygen remaining is 0.180−0.150=0.0300 mol.

questions.question: Deduce water of crystallisation from supplied masses
questions.subtopic: Ionic formula mass, significant figures, limitation, hydrated salt and back titration
questions.prompt: A sample of magnesium sulfate hydrate MgSO₄·xH₂O has mass 6.15 g. The remaining anhydrous MgSO₄ is 3.00 g. Find x using Ar Mg=24.3, S=32.1, O=16.0, H=1.0. Explain the whole-number ratio reasoning; no practical method is required. [6 marks]
markPoints: Finds mass of water=6.15−3.00=3.15 g.
Finds moles MgSO₄=3.00/120.4≈0.0249 mol.
Finds moles H₂O=3.15/18.0=0.175 mol.
Divides water moles by salt moles to get ratio≈7.02:1, rounded to whole-number 7:1.
Concludes x=7 and formula MgSO₄·7H₂O.
questions.modelAnswer: Water mass=6.15−3.00=3.15 g. Mᵣ(MgSO₄)=120.4, so n(MgSO₄)=3.00/120.4=0.0249169 mol. n(H₂O)=3.15/18.0=0.175 mol. Ratio water:salt=0.175/0.0249169≈7.02:1, giving x=7. The hydrate is MgSO₄·7H₂O. Whole-number coefficients express the formula-unit ratio.

questions.question: Interpret back-titration data for calcium carbonate content
questions.subtopic: Ionic formula mass, significant figures, limitation, hydrated salt and back titration
questions.prompt: A 1.20 g tablet containing calcium carbonate reacts with 50.0 cm³ of 0.500 mol dm⁻³ HCl. The remaining acid is represented in 100.0 cm³ of solution. A 25.0 cm³ portion of this requires 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH for neutralisation. Assuming no other acid-reactive tablet components, calculate the original mass of CaCO₃ and the percentage by mass in the tablet. Use Mᵣ(CaCO₃)=100.1 and CaCO₃+2HCl→CaCl₂+CO₂+H₂O. [8 marks]
markPoints: Initial HCl amount 0.500×50.0/1000=0.0250 mol.
Uses 1:1 neutralisation to find 0.00200 mol HCl in the 25.0 cm³ portion.
Scales to the full 100.0 cm³ remaining acid: 4×0.00200=0.00800 mol HCl.
Finds HCl consumed by the CaCO₃=0.0250−0.00800=0.0170 mol.
Uses CaCO₃:HCl=1:2 to find n(CaCO₃)=0.00850 mol.
Calculates mass percentage=(0.85085/1.20)×100≈70.9%.
questions.modelAnswer: Initially n(HCl)=0.500×0.0500=0.0250 mol. The NaOH neutralising the 25.0 cm³ aliquot is 0.100×0.0200=0.00200 mol, hence 0.00200 mol residual HCl in that aliquot. The 100.0 cm³ represents four aliquots, giving 0.00800 mol HCl left. Acid consumed=0.0250−0.00800=0.0170 mol. From CaCO₃+2HCl, n(CaCO₃)=0.0170/2=0.00850 mol; mass=0.00850×100.1=0.85085≈0.851 g. Percentage in the 1.20 g tablet=0.85085/1.20×100≈70.9%. The assumed absence of other acid-reactive substances matters.
